sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), which aligns a student model's token-level distribution with that of its self-teacher prompted by privileged context, has emerged as a promising direction to mitigate reward sparsity in sequence-level post-training paradigms. However, OPSD often fails to achieve continuous performance gains during training. In this paper, we find that the model's limited self-teaching capability underlies this phenomenon by generating unreliable guidance on certain samples. To address this problem, we propose Teacher-Evolution Self-Distillation (TESD), which enables the self-teacher to generate rollouts and receive environmental feedback based on task correctness and context independence. First, using these rewards as training objectives, we perform teacher-oriented optimization to continuously enhance the model's self-teaching capability during distillation. Second, by estimating teacher guidance reliability from these rewards, we apply adaptive student-oriented optimization to down-weight samples with unreliable guidance. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and model scales show that TESD consistently outperforms representative token-level and sequence-level methods, highlighting the necessity of improving supervision quality in OPSD.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Post-training has emerged as crucial stage for enhancing the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs) (Achiam et al., 2023; Kumar et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2026a). Among various post-training techniques, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has proven to be practical paradigm in domains where model outcomes can be automatically verified (Shao et al., 2024). Despite achieving strong performance, representative RLVR methods assign Corresponding authors. 1 Figure 1: (a) In OPSD, the self-teacher provides guidance indiscriminately across all samples without improving its own capabilities, thereby degrading the quality of supervision delivered to the student. (b) TESD improves the self-teacher using the environmental rewards of its rollouts while delivering adaptive guidance by down-weighting samples with unreliable supervision. (c) TESD achieves more continuous performance improvement than current OPSD methods. the same reward to all tokens within response. This sparse sequence-level scheme overlooks the varying significance of individual tokens, hindering the models ability to focus on important tokens during optimization (Li et al., 2026). To address this limitation, On-Policy SelfDistillation (OPSD) offers dense supervision by introducing self-teacher as shown in Figure 1 (Zhao et al., 2026b; Shenfeld et al., 2026). The selfteacher is constructed by prompting the student with self-generated privileged context, which usually consists of correct solution to the input query. By computing the per-token logits of the self-teacher on the students rollouts, OPSD delivers token-level supervision while preserving the onpolicy property. Therefore, it can maintain alignment between the dense supervision signal and the models current behavior (Hübotter et al., 2026). However, existing OPSD methods fail to continuously improve performance during training (Yang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), leading to suboptimal results as shown in Figure 1(c). This phenomenon is correlated with their reliance on the assumption of the models strong self-teaching ability, i.e., the self-teacher can always correctly guide diverse student rollouts based on the limited privileged context. First, this assumption deviates from practical implementations. The self-teacher only has the additional privileged context compared to the student, without any improvements in model capability. Thus, the self-teacher may fail to associate the limited privileged context with diverse student rollouts (Yu et al., 2026), leading to unreliable guidance. This insufficient self-teaching capability also struggles to improve during training, as the current OPSD paradigm optimizes the model solely as student. Second, relying on this unrealistic assumption, current methods overlook the teachers potential to deliver unreliable guidance on certain samples. Consequently, the student is forced to follow the teachers guidance across all samples indiscriminately (Hübotter et al., 2026), thereby injecting misleading signals into its optimization process. These two problems limit the quality of supervision received by the student, making it difficult for OPSD to achieve continuous performance improvement during the distillation process. In this paper, we propose the Teacher-Evolution Self-Distillation (TESD) framework to enhance the supervision quality of OPSD. As shown in Figure 1(b), rather than generating rollouts only through the student, TESD enables the self-teacher to generate rollouts and receive rewards. Based on these rewards, TESD introduces two complementary mechanisms to address the aforementioned problems: teacher-oriented optimization to improve the models self-teaching ability, and adaptive student-oriented optimization to mitigate the impact of unreliable teacher guidance. Specifically, for the reward function, we design it with both task-correctness and context-independence to estimate the models self-teaching ability. For teacheroriented optimization, these rewards serve directly as training objectives for the self-teacher. This objective encourages the self-teacher to generate correct and distinct solutions from privileged contexts, thereby improving its ability to associate the privileged context with diverse student rollouts. For adaptive student-oriented optimization, these rewards reflect the reliability of teacher guidance across different samples and serve as sample-wise weights that adaptively scale the students loss values. By suppressing gradient updates from samples with unreliable guidance, their negative impact on student optimization can be mitigated. In experiments, we evaluate the effectiveness of TESD on pre-trained LLMs (Yang et al., 2025; Olmo et al., 2025) with different parameter sizes and multiple downstream tasks (Feng et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2023; Jain et al., 2025). The evaluation results show that TESD consistently outperforms current representative OPSD (Hübotter et al., 2026) and sequence-level RLVR (Shao et al., 2024) methods. The superior performance of TESD demonstrates the significance of improving supervision quality during the self-distillation process. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce TESD, an OPSD framework that allows the self-teacher to generate rollouts and receive rewards regarding task correctness and context independence. With the rewards from teacher rollouts, we enhance OPSDs supervision quality through teacher-oriented and adaptive student-oriented optimization, explicitly improving the model across its dual roles as teacher and student. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of TESD, which reflects the importance of enhancing the supervision quality in the OPSD paradigm.

sections.title: 2.1 RL with Verifiable Rewards
sections.content: RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has been widely used to improve the reasoning ability of pre-trained LLMs (Guo et al., 2025). As representative RLVR method, GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) estimates group-relative advantages from sampled responses and removes the need for separate critic model. Subsequent studies further improve the GRPO by modifying the objective (Chu et al., 2025), normalization (Yu et al., 2025a), and clipping (Zhao et al., 2026b). Despite differences in training strategies and loss formulations, these methods uniformly utilize sequence-level rewards to optimize the model as student, which 2 is prompted solely by input queries. In contrast, we design reward function incorporating taskcorrectness and context-independence terms to optimize the model as self-teacher, which receives both the input query and privileged context. By optimizing the self-teacher with this reward, we leverage sequence-level feedback to enhance the supervision quality of the token-level OPSD.

sections.title: 2.2 On-Policy Self-Distillation
sections.content: Unlike classical knowledge distillation, which forces the student to strictly fit the teachers output trajectory (Gu et al., 2024), on-policy distillation (OPD) enables the teacher to provide guidance based on the students trajectory (Agarwal et al., 2024; Lu and Lab, 2025). This approach can transfer the teachers token-level knowledge while preserving the distribution of the student, making it widely adopted in LLM post-training (Yang et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2026). Building upon this, the on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) paradigm guides the student using self-teacher, which is built by prompting the student with privileged contexts, thereby achieving OPD without the external teacher (Hübotter et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026a; Shenfeld et al., 2026). However, the OPSD paradigm fails to achieve performance improvement continuously during training. To tackle this problem, current studies suggest incorporating more privileged context (Yu et al., 2026), degrading OPSD as weighted module of GRPO (Yang et al., 2026), and implementing an entropy-based routing update strategy (Jin et al., 2026). Different from these studies relying solely on studentgenerated rollouts, we empower the self-teacher to generate rollouts and obtain rewards from the environment. Using these rewards, we optimize the self-teacher and adaptively adjust the intensity of its sample-wise supervision, thereby achieving more consistent performance gains over existing methods through enhanced supervision quality.

sections.title: 3.2 Teaching Ability Investigation
sections.content: Given that all supervision signals in the training objective of Equation 1 are exclusively generated by the self-teacher πθ( x, c, ys <t), its teaching ability is crucial to the success of the OPSD paradigm. At the top of Figure 2, we investigate this ability via the correlation between the self-teachers confidence in student rollouts and their verifiable rewards. This correlation reveals whether the selfteacher can assign high confidence to correct rollouts and low confidence to incorrect ones. Moreover, we visualize the similarity between each rollout and its privileged context. The normalized edit distance is selected as the similarity metric following previous studies (Zheng et al., 2023). First, we find that the self-teacher struggles to distinguish Figure 3: Overall framework of TESD. Given an input query, the student first generates rollouts, which provide the privileged context for the self-teacher. Then, TESD optimizes the student and the self-teacher, respectively. For the self-teacher, it interacts with the environment and learns from the obtained rewards of correctness and independence. For the student, it is supervised by the logits of the self-teacher. The loss value is adaptively weighted by the teachers mean reward of the corresponding input query, which estimates the quality of teacher guidance. the correctness of student rollouts, as it assigns low confidence (0.00.5) to certain correct rollouts, while giving high confidence (0.50.8) to substantial number of incorrect ones. Second, the self-teacher tends to assign higher confidence to rollouts that resemble the privileged context. This confidence-resemblance bias is supported by the observation that high-confidence rollouts tend to have smaller edit distances from the privileged context, while large number of correct yet contextdissimilar rollouts are assigned low confidence. Furthermore, we track the evolution of selfteaching ability during the training process at the bottom of Figure 2. Rather than improving as the training progresses, the self-teachers ability exhibits downward trend coupled with significant instability. The results demonstrate that only student-oriented optimization in Equation 1 is insufficient for improving the models teaching ability. This stagnant or declining teaching ability acts as bottleneck, preventing the OPSD from obtaining continuous performance improvements. According to the above analysis, the self-teacher faces challenge in providing reliable guidance on student rollouts, and this challenge does not diminish as training progresses. This phenomenon emphasizes the importance of improving the quality of supervision received by the student.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Models and Datasets. Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B (Yang et al., 2025) and Olmo3-7B-Instruct (Olmo et al., 2025) are selected as the base models. For datasets, we train models separately on six datasets following the prior work (Hübotter et al., 2026). The first four datasets are question-answering benchmarks from the reasoning subset (L3) of SciKnowEval (Feng et al., 2024), which cover scientific reasoning in Chemistry, Physics, Biology, and Materials Science. Moreover, we use tool-use dataset from ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023), where the model is required to map tool-API specification and user request to the correct tool call. Additionally, we adopt the v6 subset of LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025), set of coding problems ranging from simple to competition-level. Each dataset is split into training set and test set. Furthermore, we evaluate the model across several holdout tasks to measure the ability of TESD to mitigate catastrophic forgetting (Zhou et al., 2023; Verschueren et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2022; Cobbe et al., 2021; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Clark et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). Baselines. We compare TESD with two baselines using the standard RLVR setting (Hübotter et al., 2026). First, we adopt strengthened implementation of GRPO in accordance with recent best practices (Khatri et al., 2025). This implementation integrates recent refinements to GRPO, such as asymmetric clipping (Yu et al., 2025b), unbiased normalization (Liu et al., 2025), and offpolicy correction for efficient inference-based rollout generation (Yao et al., 2025). Second, we utilize SDPO (Hübotter et al., 2026), representative OPSD method that functions in the same verifieronly RLVR setting as our method. sections.title: 4.2 Performance on Downstream Tasks
sections.content: Learning without rich feedback. In Table 1, we evaluate the effectiveness of TESD on tasks without rich feedback, i.e., only one correct student rollout is selected as the privileged context. First, we observe that although SDPO is claimed to achieve faster convergence through the token-level supervision (Hübotter et al., 2026), substantial performance gap remains compared to the sequencelevel GRPO upon full convergence (e.g., 69.66% vs. 73.40% on Qwen3-4B). Second, when SDPO and GRPO are directly combined, the resulting performance lies between that of the two individual methods (e.g., 72.27% vs. 74.94% on Qwen3-8B). This phenomenon indicates that naive summation at the loss level fails to promote mutual enhancement. Finally, TESD outperforms all aforementioned baselines across different base models. Learning with rich feedback. In Table 2, we present the performance of TESD and other baselines on the task with rich feedback, i.e., the privileged context including correct student rollout and other code execution results such as runtime errors and failed unit tests. First, SDPO can outperform GRPO with rich feedback, reflecting the importance of the information density within the privileged context for OPSD. Second, combining SDPO and GRPO achieves the best performance on Qwen3-1.7B, yet lags behind TESD on larger model scales (Qwen3-4B/8B). This discrepancy stems from the limited capability of Qwen31.7B, where direct supervision of the student effectively accelerates its convergence. In contrast, for stronger models, integrating the self-teacher into the optimization framework improves the quality of supervision signals and then achieves better performance. Finally, TESD consistently outperforms SDPO and GRPO across different base models, indicating that the effectiveness of TESD is compatible with the expansion of privileged context. Performance on Holdout Tasks. We evaluate the catastrophic forgetting of the model on other tasks after being trained with different methods on specific task. As Table 3 shows, TESD learns the new task while mitigating the degradation of initial capabilities, achieving better performanceforgetting tradeoff than SDPO and GRPO.

First, applying sequencelevel optimization to the student can improve the performance of OPSD (67.06% vs. 70.61%), highlighting the necessity of leveraging environment feedback. Second, optimizing the self-teacher using sequence loss achieves performance improvements over OPSD (67.06% vs. 69.35%), yet fails to outperform optimizing the student (70.61% vs. 69.35%). This is because training only with correctness reward encourages the teacher to copy the privileged context as the answer, thereby undermining its ability to guide diverse student rollouts. By introducing reward term based on edit distance in Equation 2, this copying behavior can be effectively mitigated, thereby enhancing the teachers ability and resulting in enhanced performance. Adaptive Loss Weighting. As shown in Table 5, we investigate the effectiveness of the proposed weighting mechanism on three datasets of the SciKnowEval benchmark using Qwen3-8B. We observe that directly weighting the distillation loss of input queries using the mean reward in Equation 2 leads to performance degradation (69.53% vs. 73.76%). Introducing softmax normalization alleviates this issue, yet the performance remains worse than the unweighted baseline with teacheroriented optimization (70.56% vs. 73.76%). After incorporating scaling and clipping, significant performance boost is achieved (75.49% vs. 70.56%). This result not only validates the effectiveness of the proposed weighting mechanism but also reveals the importance of maintaining the overall scale of loss values during the weighting process. Additional ablations of the rollout numbers and λedit are provided in the supplementary materials.

sections.title: 4.4 Analysis
sections.content: Model Uncertainty. We explore the impact of TESD on the models uncertainty through the accuracy standard deviation and response length of the model. Experiments are conducted on the Physics subset of SciKnowEval using Qwen3-8B. First, as Figure 4(a) shows, both GRPO and TESD maintain higher accuracy standard deviation compared to SDPO. Second, for response length in Figure 4(b), GRPO exhibits an increasing trend as training progresses, while SDPO shows rapid decline in the early training stages before stabilizing. TESD falls between these two trajectories, presenting gradual decrease in both metrics. These results indicate that, compared to SDPO, TESD tends to maintain more uncertainty in model outputs and prevents the over-confidence phenomenon during training. Meanwhile, TESD preserves key characteristic of the OPSD paradigm: it attempts to generate shorter responses rather than relying on extended reasoning paths to boost performance like GRPO. Teaching Ability. For the teaching ability, we adopt the same metric as in Figure 2. As shown in Figure 4(c), integrating the self-teacher into the optimization framework can gradually enhance its ability during training. Moreover, we find that the teaching ability in TESD exhibits greater stabil7 Figure 4: We report the evolution of the standard deviation of accuracy across 16 evaluations (a), the models average response length (b), teaching ability (c), and the distillation loss (d) across the training process. Figure 5: Token-level teacher credit heatmaps of SDPO and TESD with Qwen3-8B on the Physics dataset. ity (as reflected by smaller local variance), while SDPO suffers from severe fluctuations. Additionally, we present the distillation loss in Figure 4(d). Compared to SDPO, TESD shows higher losses during the middle and late stages of training. By optimizing the self-teacher, it can continuously provide significant guidance during training. As result, the student is prevented from overfitting to an unoptimized self-teacher in the early stages, pitfall that typically leads to performance stagnation in later phases. Furthermore, we provide qualitative analysis in Figure 5. In contrast to SDPO, which strongly supervises almost every token, TESD exhibits sparser pattern. It diminishes the focus on common words like "a", "the", and "of", allowing the model to focus primarily on query-relevant keywords such as "ionization", "gas", and "E_{Ar}". Evolution of Adaptive Weights. In Figure 6, we investigate the distribution of the mean teacher reward (Equation 4) and the corresponding adaptive weight (Equation 5) within the input batch during training. In the early stages of training, due to the weak ability of the self-teacher, the adaptive mechanism decreases the loss of samples with unreliable teacher guidance to around 0.5. As teacher-oriented optimization improves the self-teacher over time, the teacher reward rises with the adaptive weights shifting toward 1.0. These results demonstrate the complementary relationship between the teacherFigure 6: Distributions of the mean reward (top) and the adaptive weight (bottom) of the input batch. oriented and the adaptive student-oriented optimization throughout the training process. Additional case studies and training time analysis are provided in the supplementary materials.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we propose method called TeacherEvolution Self-Distillation (TESD) to achieve on-policy self-distillation with continuous performance improvements by enhancing the quality of the self-teachers supervision. First, we design reward function considering both correctness and independence to evaluate the self-teachers ability to guide diverse student rollouts. Then, using this reward, we perform teacher-oriented optimization to improve the models self-teaching capability during training. Finally, we utilize this reward for adaptive student-oriented optimization, which suppresses updates on queries with potentially unreliable teacher supervision. Extensive experiments indicate the stronger performance of TESD compared to representative OPSD methods, indicating the importance of enhancing the supervision quality. In future, we will investigate the optimization geometry of TESD and apply it to other domains such as multimodal reasoning (Shen et al., 2026b).

sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content: A.1.1 Training Strategies All methods are implemented on top of the verl framework (Sheng et al., 2024) and trained with FSDP on single 8H20 node. All training rollouts use temperature =1.0, top-p=1.0, topk=1 with sampling enabled. The thinking mode of the Qwen3 family is disabled. Inputs and responses are bounded by 2048 and 8192 tokens, respectively. All methods use AdamW (β1=0.9, β2=0.999) with weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping at 1.0, constant learning-rate schedule with 10 warmup steps, and 1 PPO epoch per iteration. The training batch size is 32 prompts per step. Checkpoint and validation frequency are set to every 200 and 10 training steps, respectively. We train the model for 30 epochs on both the science question-answering tasks and for 15 epochs on the ToolUse task. For LCBv6, we train the model for 40 steps across all methods. For GRPO, we sample 16 rollouts per prompt with mini-batch size of 8. The policygradient loss adopts asymmetric PPO clipping with ϵlow=0.2, ϵhigh=0.28 and dual-clip lower bound c=3.0. To support efficient inference-based rollout generation, we apply token-level truncated importance-sampling (IS) correction with threshold of 2.0. No KL penalty is used. The learning rate is selected from 1e-5 and 1e-6 based on validation performance. For SDPO, we adopt its official implementa12 Figure 10: Teacher input template. tions (Hübotter et al., 2026). The self-teacher is maintained as an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student with an update rate of 0.05. The distillation loss is the generalized Jensen Shannon divergence over the full logit distribution, approximated by the top-100 logits with an explicit tail bucket. The distillation importance-sampling ratio is clipped at 2.0. The same asymmetric clipping and token-level IS correction as in the GRPO baseline are applied to the student policy. Successful student rollouts are selected as the privileged context, with the self-success exclusion enabled and thinking traces removed from the demonstration. For TESD, it samples 8 student rollouts and 8 teacher rollouts. The teacher reward follows Eq. (2): task correctness Rtask {0, 1} minus an independence reward λedit Redit. Redit [0, 1] is the token-level normalized edit distance computed using the SequenceMatcher of difflib package in Python. λedit is set as 1.0 across all experiments. The EMA teacher update rate is reduced to 0.01 for stabilizing the training process. For the adaptive student-oriented optimization (Eq. 57), the weight wx is computed with temperature τ =1.0, then clipped to [0.05, 5.0]. Table 6 summarizes the method-specific hyperparameters. For each test problem, we sample 16 responses with temperature of 0.6 and top-p = 0.95, and report the mean accuracy (mean@16), i.e., the fraction of correct responses averaged over the 16 samples. The final reported metric is the maximum mean@16 observed across the training trajectory, ensuring fair comparison of convergence upper bounds. The task correctness reward Rtask is rule-based and task-specific: SciKnowEval (multiple-choice questions): The model is prompted to output the option letter inside the <answer>...</answer> tags via system instruction. We extract the letter inside the tags and set Rtask = 1 if it matches the ground-truth option, and 0 otherwise. ToolUse: Given tool-API specification and user request, the model generates ThoughtAction-Action_Input trace. We set Rtask = 1 if the model prediction matches the groundtruth tool call, and 0 otherwise. LCBv6 (coding problems): The model outputs Python program in fenced code block. We set Rtask = 1 if the program passes all hidden test cases within the time limit in sandbox environment, and 0 otherwise. For hold-out task evaluation in Table 3 of the main paper, we evaluate the final converged checkpoint of each method on eight hold-out tasks. For IFEval, MMLU-Pro, TruthfulQA, ARCChallenge, HumanEval, and HaluEval, we utilize the lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024) framework with generation budget of 32768 tokens and greedy decoding. We apply the models default settings for the chat template, except for HumanEval, where generation is performed in the raw completion format. ARC-Challenge is evaluated in the multiple-choice setting. Regarding the evaluation metrics, IFEval reports strict instructionfollowing accuracy, MMLU-Pro and TruthfulQA report exact-match accuracy, HumanEval reports pass@1, and HaluEval reports exact-match accuracy for hallucination avoidance on the dialogue subset. For mathematical reasoning tasks (MATH500 and GSM8K), we evaluate using temperature of 0.6 and top-p = 1.0, reporting pass@1. Answers are extracted and normalized before comparison with the ground truth. A.1.3 Prompt Templates Following SDPO (Hübotter et al., 2026), we use the same dataset prompts for student rollout and evaluation. For Qwen models, we disable the thinkingmode chat-template option during prompt construction. The concrete ScienceQA and ToolUse prompt templates are shown in Figures 7, 8, and 9. Experiments are conducted on SciKnowEval benchmark using Qwen3-4B over 10 training epochs. SDPO does not improve significantly with the increasing number of rollouts (e.g., when increases from 32 to 48, the performance drops from 55.25% to 55.12%). In contrast, the performance of TESD improves consistently as the number of rollouts grows. This demonstrates that, by allocating partial rollout computation to the self-teacher, TESD can more effectively leverage increased training time to yield consistent performance gains. A.2.2 Qualitative Results In Figure 11, we present the responses generated by models trained with different methods. First, compared to OPSD methods, GRPO generates significantly longer responses that contain large amount of redundant reasoning (such as repetitive "wait" tokens), leading to wasted computations. Second, while SDPO produces shorter answers, it lacks genuine reasoning depth, dedicating numerous tokens to excessive self-affirmations. This phenomenon highlights the overconfidence issue inherent in existing OPSD paradigms (Li et al., 2026). Finally, in contrast to both methods, TESD successfully solves the problems with concise responses dominated almost entirely by effective, substance-driven reasoning. A.2.3 Effects of λedit In Table 9, we investigate the impact of the hyperparameter λedit in Equation 2 on the performance of TESD. First, we observe that different subsets require different optimal values for λedit. For instance, the optimal λedit is 1.0 for the biology subset and 0.7 for the materials subset. Second, setting λedit = 1.0 achieves the highest average performance across all three subsets. Therefore, to avoid dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning, we fix λedit = 1.0 for all main experiments. Figure 12: The time cost of different methods during the training process. Experiments are conducted on the LCBv6 benchmark using Qwen3-8B. A.2.4 Training Efficiency In Figure 12, we compare the time cost of different methods on the LCBv6 benchmark. We observe that as training progresses, TESD requires increasingly less time compared to GRPO and SDPO. This efficiency gain arises because substantial portion of the training time in coding tasks is consumed by code execution and sandbox evaluation. Since TESD better enhances the models capabilities throughout the training process, it generates programs that are more structured and efficient to execute, thereby accelerating training speed. sections.title: Privileged Context
sections.content: Recently, several concurrent studies have improved OPSD from the perspective of privileged context by increasing its volume (Yu et al., 2026) or strengthening it through contrastive exemplars (Pan et al., 2026). In this section, we discuss the similarities and differences between them. Similarity. Both TESD and these concurrent methods identify the quality of teacher guidance as the primary bottleneck that constrains the performance of the OPSD paradigm, and actively seek to improve it. Difference. While these concurrent methods focus heavily on the quality of the context provided to the self-teacher, TESD focuses on the self-teachers inherent capability to leverage this context to effectively guide diverse student rollouts. These two paradigms stabilize the performance gains of OPSD from complementary angles, suggesting promising potential for integration. 15 via an exponential moving average to ensure training stability. This mechanism inherently smooths out the improvement of the teachers capabilities, thereby limiting the speed at which the teacher evolves. In the future, to address these limitations, we will attempt to develop an adaptive independence term for the teacher reward and investigate the internal mechanism of the relationship between teacher updates and training stability. Moreover, investigating whether TESD exhibits sparse update patterns (Shen et al., 2024, 2026c) offers an interesting direction for further understanding the studentteacher co-evolution framework. sections.title: GRPO and SDPO
sections.content: Several concurrent studies have explored combining token-level OPSD with sequence-level GRPO (Yang et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026). In this section, we discuss both the similarities and differences between TESD and these approaches. Similarity. Both TESD and these methods integrate supervision at both the sequence level and token level. Difference. (i) For the motivation, these concurrent studies degrade OPSD to an advantage-weighting component within GRPO. Conversely, TESD leverages GRPO to empower the self-teacher for improving OPSDs supervision quality. (ii) For the loss formulation, these studies adopt the standard GRPO objective, while TESD preserves the divergence-based loss of OPSD for the (iii) For the optimization student model. framework, these studies apply the GRPO and OPSD to single student model. In contrast, TESD differentiates the models dual roles, utilizing GRPO with specifically designed rewards for the self-teacher and OPSD with proposed adaptive weighting mechanism for the student, offering principled framework rather than naive objective blend. A.4 Ethical Considerations This work aims to improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models. We acknowledge that enhanced reasoning capabilities could also be misused for harmful purposes. Therefore, we emphasize the importance of deploying such models with robust safety alignment mechanisms to mitigate potential risks. All datasets used in our experiments are publicly available open-source resources. We adhere to their respective licenses and use them in accordance with their intended purposes. A.4.1 Limitations Despite outperforming representative token-level and sequence-level methods, TESD introduces additional hyperparameters, such as λedit, due to the inclusion of extra training objectives and rewards.
